messages.content: I want to develop a semantic parser that distinguishes genuine utterance ambiguity from model uncertainty when it encounters unseen compositional structures. What is the central distinction?

Genuine utterance ambiguity means the utterance has more than one valid interpretation. Model uncertainty means the parser is unsure what interpretation to assign; that uncertainty alone does not establish that multiple interpretations are valid. The goal is to keep those two situations separate, including on compositions the parser has not seen before.
So if the parser hesitates over an unfamiliar composition, that hesitation is not enough to label the utterance ambiguous?

Right. Unfamiliarity may leave the parser unsure, but the ambiguity judgment must concern the utterance’s valid interpretations, not just the parser’s confidence. An unfamiliar composition could still be unambiguous.
And the reverse matters too: the parser might feel confident even though an utterance admits multiple interpretations?

Yes. Confidence in one interpretation would not, by itself, rule out another valid interpretation. The intended distinction is about what the utterance permits, rather than how certain the model feels about its preferred output.
How should the ambiguity-detection requirement be stated precisely?

The target is ambiguity-detection F1 of at least 0.85 on unseen compositions, using independently annotated sets of valid interpretations. That states both the performance threshold and the basis for judging whether an utterance is genuinely ambiguous.
Why specify sets of valid interpretations rather than simply asking whether the parser produced several outputs?

Several parser outputs could reflect uncertainty or errors; they do not automatically establish that an utterance is ambiguous. Independently annotated sets of valid interpretations provide a reference separate from the parser’s own proposals. The ambiguity judgment can then turn on which interpretations are valid, rather than on how many candidates the parser happens to generate.
Does that require a particular annotation procedure?

No particular procedure is specified here. What is specified is that the sets of valid interpretations are independently annotated. The requirement does not prescribe an annotation workflow, a number of annotators, or a way of resolving disagreements.
What does the F1 threshold tell me, and what does it leave open?

It sets a minimum of F1 ≥0.85 for ambiguity detection on unseen compositions. F1 combines precision and recall, so the goal concerns the balance between identifying genuinely ambiguous utterances and avoiding incorrect ambiguity labels. It does not separately state a required precision or recall value.
I also do not want the parser to gain ambiguity detection by giving up reliable execution on inputs with only one valid interpretation.

That is the second requirement: on unambiguous inputs, its execution accuracy should match that of a single-output parser trained on identical data. Ambiguity detection is not meant to come at the expense of that comparison on unambiguous inputs.
Why is the phrase ‘trained on identical data’ important in that comparison?

It fixes the training-data condition for the single-output parser used as the baseline. The comparison is not with a parser trained on a different amount or selection of data. It does not, by itself, specify that the two parsers must share an architecture or training method.
Does ‘match’ mean the new parser has to outperform the single-output parser?
No. The stated requirement is to match its unambiguous-input execution accuracy, not to exceed it. No numerical execution-accuracy target or permitted difference is given here.
Are the ambiguity-detection F1 and the execution-accuracy comparison measuring the same thing?

No. Ambiguity-detection F1 measures how well the parser identifies genuinely ambiguous utterances on unseen compositions, against independently annotated sets of valid interpretations. The other requirement concerns execution accuracy on unambiguous inputs, compared with a single-output parser trained on identical data. Both conditions matter, but they assess different behavior.
Suppose an utterance has one independently annotated valid interpretation, but the parser entertains two candidates. How should I think about that conceptually?

Entertaining two candidates would not make the utterance genuinely ambiguous. In that situation, the extra candidate could reflect uncertainty or error on the parser’s part. The independent set of valid interpretations is what separates the property of the utterance from the parser’s internal indecision.
And if the independent set contains more than one valid interpretation, a single confident prediction would not settle the ambiguity question?

Correct. A single prediction can be confident without capturing all the valid interpretations. The ambiguity question remains whether the utterance admits multiple valid interpretations, as represented in the independently annotated set.
What role do unseen compositional structures play in the goal?

They make the distinction important beyond familiar combinations. The parser is meant to distinguish ambiguity from its own uncertainty under unseen compositional structures, and the stated F1 threshold applies on unseen compositions. The requirement does not say that unfamiliarity itself counts as ambiguity.
Does the goal specify a particular kind of semantic parser or a mechanism for expressing uncertainty?

No. It specifies the behavior to develop and the two performance requirements, but not an architecture or a particular uncertainty representation. Any discussion of a mechanism would be a proposal, not a detail already fixed by this goal.
I want to make sure ‘valid interpretations’ is doing real work here, rather than meaning anything the model can generate.

It is. The phrase refers to interpretations counted as valid in the independently annotated sets, not merely to candidate outputs generated by the parser. That distinction is essential when the parser confronts an unseen composition: producing alternatives and establishing genuine utterance ambiguity are different things.
Could strong ambiguity-detection F1 alone satisfy the whole objective?

No. The goal has two requirements. Ambiguity-detection F1 must reach at least 0.85 on unseen compositions using independently annotated sets of valid interpretations, and unambiguous-input execution accuracy must match the single-output parser trained on identical data. Meeting one condition would not, on its own, establish the other.
Then the intended parser is neither one that calls every difficult utterance ambiguous nor one that always forces a single interpretation.

That captures the intended distinction. It should identify genuine ambiguity without treating its own uncertainty as proof of ambiguity, while retaining the specified execution-accuracy comparison on unambiguous inputs. Those are objectives for development, not claims that the parser already meets them.
If I state the goal in one careful sentence, what must I keep explicit?

Keep the distinction between genuine utterance ambiguity and model uncertainty under unseen compositional structures; the ambiguity-detection target of F1 ≥0.85 on unseen compositions using independently annotated sets of valid interpretations; and the requirement to match unambiguous-input execution accuracy of a single-output parser trained on identical data.

For the parser design, I’m considering freezing a single-output execution parser and training a set-valued validity head to flag multiple supported interpretations. How would that separate ambiguity from ensemble disagreement?

The frozen parser would retain its single-output execution role, while the validity head would address a different question: which interpretations are supported by the utterance? If the head identifies multiple supported interpretations, that is a basis for an ambiguity flag. Different predictions from an ensemble, by contrast, show disagreement among models; disagreement alone does not establish that multiple interpretations are valid.
What does freezing the execution parser contribute to the proposal?

It keeps the single-output execution parser fixed while the set-valued validity head is trained. That makes execution and ambiguity assessment distinct parts of the proposal. Freezing the parser does not, by itself, prove that the full system will match the required unambiguous-input execution accuracy; that remains something to evaluate.
So the validity head is not just another single-output parser?

Right. Its proposed role is set-valued: it can identify more than one supported interpretation when an utterance genuinely permits them. The execution parser still has a single-output role. The proposal does not specify the head’s architecture or how it represents the set.
I’m wary of treating every alternative prediction as a valid alternative. Is that the main distinction?

Yes. An alternative prediction is something a model produced; a supported interpretation is one that the utterance validly permits. The validity head is proposed to distinguish those cases, so an ambiguity flag depends on multiple supported interpretations rather than merely multiple predictions.
Suppose several models choose different interpretations of an unfamiliar composition. What can I conclude from that disagreement?

You can conclude that the models disagree. You cannot conclude from disagreement alone that the utterance is genuinely ambiguous: one interpretation might be valid and the others might reflect model uncertainty or error. The proposed validity head is meant to assess support for the interpretations rather than substitute disagreement for that assessment.
Could the models agree and the utterance still be ambiguous?

Conceptually, yes. Agreement on one output would not rule out another valid interpretation that the models did not produce. That is another reason not to define ambiguity in terms of ensemble behavior alone.
Does this proposal require me to build an ensemble?

No ensemble is specified as a required component. Ensemble disagreement is the phenomenon the proposal aims to keep separate from genuine ambiguity, not a prescribed method for finding interpretations.
When I say the head should ‘flag multiple supported interpretations,’ am I asking it to mark any case where it is uncertain between candidates?

No. Uncertainty between candidates describes the model’s state; support concerns whether the utterance admits the interpretations. A set-valued validity head should not treat indecision alone as evidence that both candidates are supported.
How does the single-output parser fit if the validity head finds multiple supported interpretations?

The proposal gives them different roles. The frozen parser provides a single execution output, while the validity head can flag that more than one interpretation is supported. The proposal does not specify how to present or choose among supported interpretations in that case.
Is the idea that the validity head fixes the execution parser’s output?

That is not stated. The proposal is to freeze the single-output execution parser and train a set-valued validity head to flag multiple supported interpretations. It does not say that the head revises the parser’s output or changes how execution is performed.
What if the head supports only one interpretation even though several candidate interpretations are available?

Several available candidates would not, on their own, justify an ambiguity flag. If only one is supported, the proposed distinction treats the extra candidates as insufficient evidence of genuine utterance ambiguity. That describes the intended meaning of the flag, not a claim that the head will always judge support correctly.
And if it supports two interpretations that are genuinely valid, the flag should reflect ambiguity even if the execution parser emits only one?

Yes. A single execution output does not make the utterance unambiguous. Under this proposal, multiple supported interpretations are what the validity head is meant to flag, independently of the execution parser’s single-output role.
Does ‘set-valued’ commit us to a particular number of interpretations or a particular cutoff for support?

No number of interpretations or support cutoff is specified. ‘Set-valued’ expresses the intended ability to assess more than one interpretation as supported; the proposal leaves the exact representation and decision procedure open.
I still need the broader goal to hold on unseen compositions. Does this design establish that?

Not by itself. It is a proposed way to separate genuine ambiguity from model uncertainty, including when compositional structures are unseen. Whether it achieves ambiguity-detection F1 ≥0.85 on unseen compositions, using independently annotated sets of valid interpretations, would have to be measured. The same is true of matching the unambiguous-input execution accuracy of a single-output parser trained on identical data.
Then freezing the execution parser is a design choice intended to keep execution stable, not evidence that the accuracy comparison has already been met?
Exactly. Freezing says what happens to that parser during the proposed training of the validity head. It is not an observed result, and it does not replace the required accuracy comparison.
Can you state the proposed division of labor without making ensemble disagreement sound like a ground-truth label?

Keep a single-output execution parser frozen for execution, and train a separate set-valued validity head to identify when multiple interpretations are supported. Treat ensemble disagreement, if it occurs, as disagreement among models—not as the definition of utterance ambiguity. The head’s proposed ambiguity flag is about multiple supported interpretations.
How can the validity head recognize multiple licensed parses under unseen compositions without treating low-confidence alternatives as genuine ambiguity?

The key is to make the question about each parse’s validity, not its relative confidence. A second parse should count toward an ambiguity flag only if it is licensed by the utterance. Low confidence in the execution parser’s preferred parse, or the presence of a less-preferred alternative, does not establish that the alternative is valid. That describes the distinction the head needs to make; it does not yet specify how to train it to make that distinction reliably on unseen compositions.
If the preferred parse looks shaky, shouldn’t the head at least be more willing to flag ambiguity?

It may have reason to examine alternatives, but shakiness alone is evidence of model uncertainty, not of multiple licensed parses. The ambiguity flag should still depend on whether more than one parse is supported by the utterance. Otherwise, difficult unambiguous inputs could be mislabeled as ambiguous simply because the model finds them difficult.
What does ‘licensed’ add beyond saying that a parse is possible for the model to produce?

A model can produce a parse that does not validly interpret the utterance. ‘Licensed’ asks whether the utterance actually permits that parse, irrespective of whether the model generated it or how much confidence the model assigned it. Multiple generated candidates are therefore not the same thing as multiple licensed parses.
Would the validity head be judging the candidates against one another?

The important distinction is not merely which candidate ranks highest. A relative ranking can put one parse first and another second even when only one is licensed; it can also favor one parse when both are licensed. The head’s proposed set-valued role is to identify which parses are supported, so an ambiguity flag reflects more than one supported member of that set.
So a low-ranked parse could still matter if it is genuinely licensed?

Yes. Being less preferred by a model does not make a parse invalid. If the utterance licenses both it and another parse, that is the kind of multiplicity the head is meant to recognize. Conversely, a low-ranked parse that is merely a plausible model guess should not count toward genuine ambiguity.
Why does the unseen-composition condition make this especially hard?

Under an unseen composition, the parser may be uncertain because the combination is unfamiliar. The head must not mistake that uncertainty for a property of the utterance. It still has to distinguish a novel but singly licensed interpretation from an utterance that licenses multiple interpretations. The question does not specify a mechanism that guarantees that generalization.
If two models disagree on an unseen composition, could that serve as a shortcut for finding the ambiguous ones?

Disagreement might draw attention to a case, but it cannot settle whether both parses are licensed. The models might disagree because one is mistaken or because both are uncertain. The validity question remains about the utterance, not the number of differing model predictions.
Is the head supposed to be certain whenever it says there is only one licensed parse?

No such certainty is specified. The head can itself be uncertain. The point is that its uncertainty should not be expressed as a claim that the utterance licenses multiple parses unless there is support for that claim. A difficult judgment and a genuinely ambiguous utterance are different things.
Can you illustrate the distinction without assuming anything about a particular dataset?

In one hypothetical case, the model considers parses A and B but only A is a valid interpretation of the utterance. B’s presence reflects uncertainty or error, not ambiguity. In another, the utterance validly permits both A and B, even if the model strongly prefers A. Only the second case has the multiple licensed parses that the validity head is meant to flag.
Does the head need to know why a candidate is licensed, or is recognizing that it is licensed the whole question here?

The question here asks how the head can recognize multiple licensed parses without conflating them with low-confidence alternatives. It does not prescribe an explanation format or a particular way for the head to establish validity. Whatever approach is considered, it would need to preserve that distinction; simply assigning uncertainty to several candidates would not answer the question.
Could I define ambiguity as ‘the top two parses have similar confidence’?

That would define a pattern in model confidence, not genuine utterance ambiguity. Similar confidence can arise when the model cannot decide between a valid parse and an invalid one. Two licensed parses might also receive very different confidence levels. Confidence similarity alone therefore does not make the required distinction.
Then is ‘multiple supported interpretations’ a claim stronger than ‘I cannot confidently choose one’?

Yes. ‘I cannot confidently choose one’ describes the model’s uncertainty. ‘Multiple interpretations are supported’ makes a claim about what the utterance permits. The latter requires support for the alternatives themselves, rather than just doubt about the preferred output.
How should I think about independent annotations in relation to this question?

Independently annotated sets of valid interpretations provide a way to evaluate whether the head’s ambiguity judgments track licensed interpretations rather than its own confidence. They do not, by their mere existence, explain how the head will generalize that distinction to unseen compositions. That remains the substance of the question.
If a case is novel and the head cannot tell whether a second parse is licensed, should I call that ambiguity?

Not solely because it cannot tell. That describes uncertainty about the second parse’s validity. Calling the utterance genuinely ambiguous would assert that the second parse is licensed. The open challenge is to avoid making that assertion on the basis of uncertainty alone while still recognizing cases where multiple parses really are licensed.
So the hard part is not producing alternatives; it is deciding which alternatives belong in the valid set when the composition is unseen?

Exactly. Producing or encountering alternatives does not answer whether they belong in the set of licensed parses. The validity head’s proposed role puts that judgment at the center, especially where unfamiliar composition can make unsupported alternatives look tempting.
Can we claim that separating the execution parser from the validity head solves that hard part?

No. The separation makes their roles clear: one supplies a single execution output, and the other is meant to identify supported interpretations. It does not establish that the validity head can recognize multiple licensed parses under unseen compositions, or that it will avoid mistaking low-confidence alternatives for ambiguity. Those are the unresolved abilities the question asks about.
What is the most careful way to phrase the question we still need to answer?

How can the set-valued validity head identify when an unseen composition licenses more than one parse, while withholding an ambiguity judgment when additional parses merely reflect the model’s low confidence? That keeps the focus on validity of interpretations rather than on uncertainty or disagreement.

Here is a hypothesis: set-supervised validity scores trained with compositional counterfactual negatives could reject ensemble-only alternatives, achieve ambiguity-detection F1 ≥0.85, and avoid degrading frozen-decoder execution. Does that address the question about unseen compositions?

It proposes an answer, but it remains a hypothesis. Set supervision would orient the validity scores toward which interpretations belong in a valid set, while compositional counterfactual negatives would challenge the head to reject alternatives that are not licensed. The predicted outcome is that ensemble disagreement alone would not trigger an ambiguity judgment, including under unseen compositions. The F1 and execution claims would still need to be tested.
What do you mean by ‘set-supervised’ in this hypothesis?

It means the validity scores are trained with supervision about sets of valid interpretations, rather than treating the parser’s single preferred output as the complete account of what the utterance permits. The hypothesis does not specify a scoring formula or training objective.
Why are compositional counterfactual negatives part of it?

Their proposed role is to give the validity head alternatives to reject when evaluating compositional structures. The important distinction is that an alternative can be available—or even favored by a disagreeing model—without being licensed by the utterance. The hypothesis does not specify how those negatives are constructed.
Would an ensemble-only alternative mean an interpretation that some model predicts but that is not genuinely supported?

Yes, that captures the intended contrast. ‘Ensemble-only’ points to an alternative arising from model disagreement, not one established as a valid interpretation. The hypothesis predicts that the validity scores will reject such alternatives rather than count them as evidence of utterance ambiguity.
But the head must not reject a genuinely valid second parse just because it is not the execution parser’s choice.

Correct. The hypothesis requires both sides of that distinction: reject unsupported alternatives while retaining interpretations that are genuinely licensed. Otherwise, it might avoid false ambiguity flags only by missing real ambiguity, which would not establish the proposed ambiguity-detection performance.
Is low confidence itself what the counterfactual negatives are meant to detect?

Not exactly. The proposed negatives are about invalid alternatives, whereas low confidence is a property of a model’s judgment. The hypothesis is that training validity scores to distinguish valid sets from compositional counterfactual negatives will help prevent uncertainty or ensemble disagreement from being mistaken for multiple valid interpretations.
How strong is the F1 claim?

The predicted threshold is ambiguity-detection F1 ≥0.85, in the goal’s setting of unseen compositions. It is a proposed outcome, not an achieved score. Independent annotations of valid-interpretation sets would provide the reference for assessing ambiguity detection; the hypothesis itself supplies no measurements.
And ‘without degrading frozen-decoder execution’ is also a prediction, not an observed result?

Yes. Freezing the single-output execution parser motivates the expectation that training the validity head will not degrade its execution behavior, but the absence of degradation is still part of the hypothesis. It should not be reported as a demonstrated accuracy result.
Does freezing the decoder guarantee that overall unambiguous-input execution accuracy matches the single-output baseline?

No guarantee follows from the hypothesis alone. The relevant goal is to match unambiguous-input execution accuracy of a single-output parser trained on identical data. The hypothesis predicts no degradation of frozen-decoder execution, but whether the resulting system satisfies that comparison is an empirical question.
Could the head achieve a high ambiguity F1 while failing to reject ensemble-only alternatives?

The hypothesis specifically predicts rejection of ensemble-only alternatives as part of how it separates genuine ambiguity from model disagreement. An aggregate F1 value alone would not explain every individual judgment. To assess this particular claim, one would need to examine whether alternatives supported only by ensemble disagreement are treated as invalid rather than as extra licensed parses.
What if the scores reject everything except the frozen decoder’s output? That would avoid ensemble-only false positives.

It could avoid some false positives, but it would not fulfill the hypothesis’s intended distinction if it also rejected genuinely licensed additional parses. Set-supervised validity scores are proposed to recognize the valid set, which may contain multiple interpretations, not merely to endorse the decoder’s single output.
So this is not a proposal to use ensemble votes as ambiguity labels?

Right. Ensemble disagreement is precisely what the validity scores are meant to keep separate from genuine ambiguity. The hypothesis does not equate a vote for an interpretation with evidence that the utterance licenses it.
How does the compositional aspect relate to the unseen-composition requirement without assuming the training negatives cover every future combination?

The hypothesis is that training with compositional counterfactual negatives helps the validity head make the licensed-versus-unsupported distinction on unseen compositions. It does not assert that training covers every possible composition, nor does it provide a guarantee of generalization. Achieving F1 ≥0.85 there is the predicted outcome to evaluate.
Can we say exactly what a counterfactual negative looks like?

Not from this hypothesis. It identifies compositional counterfactual negatives as a training ingredient, but gives no construction rule or example tied to a particular semantic-parser domain. The safe claim is about their intended role as alternatives whose validity scores should be low, not about a specific way to generate them.
What is the relationship between a validity score and an ambiguity flag here?

The scores are intended to support a set-valued judgment about which interpretations are licensed. An ambiguity flag would reflect multiple supported interpretations, rather than merely low confidence in one output or disagreement between models. The hypothesis does not fix a numerical score threshold or a decision rule for turning scores into that flag.
If the validity head is uncertain about a second parse, does the hypothesis tell us to count it as valid?

No. Its central prediction is that unsupported alternatives, including ensemble-only ones, will be rejected rather than promoted to genuine ambiguity because the head is uncertain. How uncertain cases are handled operationally is not specified; uncertainty alone should not be recast as a licensed second parse.
Could you separate the proposed mechanism from the predicted outcomes in plain language?

The proposed mechanism is to train set-supervised validity scores using compositional counterfactual negatives, while keeping the single-output execution decoder frozen. The predicted outcomes are that the head rejects alternatives arising only from ensemble disagreement, reaches ambiguity-detection F1 ≥0.85 on unseen compositions, and does so without degrading frozen-decoder execution. None of those outcomes is asserted as already observed.
What would it mean if the head rejected an ensemble-only alternative but also missed a valid alternative?

It would show why rejection alone is not the full objective. The head must distinguish unsupported alternatives from licensed ones; rejecting both would undermine ambiguity detection. The F1 target expresses the need to detect ambiguity while avoiding incorrect ambiguity flags, rather than simply minimizing the number of alternatives it accepts.
Is there any tension between preserving execution and allowing the head to recognize multiple interpretations?

They are different roles in this hypothesis. The frozen decoder continues to produce a single execution output, while the validity head can assess a set of supported interpretations. Recognizing that a second parse is licensed need not mean changing the decoder’s output, but the hypothesis does not claim a measured absence of execution degradation.
Then the careful statement is that this training might solve the uncertainty-versus-ambiguity problem, not that it already has.

Exactly. The hypothesis is that set-supervised validity scores trained with compositional counterfactual negatives will reject ensemble-only alternatives, attain ambiguity F1 ≥0.85 on unseen compositions, and preserve frozen-decoder execution. It remains a prediction until those outcomes are evaluated.

To investigate the validity head, I want to train it on annotated interpretation sets and counterfactual negatives, calibrate it on development compositions, then evaluate unseen-composition F1 and execution parity. Does that form a coherent plan?

Yes. The training step concerns which interpretations are valid and which counterfactual alternatives should be rejected. Calibration on development compositions concerns how the head’s judgments are used to flag ambiguity. Evaluation on unseen compositions then tests whether it distinguishes multiple licensed interpretations from mere model uncertainty, alongside the separate check of execution parity. This is a plan, not an outcome.
What does an annotated interpretation set contribute that a single preferred parse would not?

A set can represent all interpretations annotated as valid for an utterance, including cases with more than one. A single preferred parse would not, by itself, tell the head whether another interpretation is also licensed. The sets therefore provide supervision for the distinction the head is supposed to make.
And what are the counterfactual negatives meant to contribute?

They give the head alternatives that should not be accepted as valid interpretations. Their role in the plan is to help it avoid treating an available alternative as a licensed one simply because a model proposed it or was uncertain. The plan does not specify how those negatives are constructed.
Would training on positives and negatives mean the head just chooses whichever interpretation scores highest?

Not necessarily. The intended judgment is set-valued: more than one interpretation may be valid. Training should support recognizing that set while rejecting unsupported alternatives, rather than forcing a choice of exactly one. The plan does not prescribe a particular scoring objective or decision rule.
How does calibration fit between training and evaluation?

Calibration on development compositions is the planned step for relating the head’s validity judgments to its ambiguity decisions before evaluating unseen compositions. It does not itself demonstrate that the decisions will generalize. No particular calibration method or numerical cutoff is specified.
Is calibration supposed to make every uncertain case count as ambiguous?

No. That would collapse the distinction the plan is meant to test. An ambiguity decision should reflect multiple licensed interpretations; uncertainty about whether an alternative is valid is not, on its own, evidence that it belongs in the valid set.
Why calibrate on development compositions rather than judging performance only where the compositions are unseen?

The plan separates adjustment from evaluation: calibrate on development compositions, then assess ambiguity detection on unseen compositions. The unseen-composition F1 is the evaluation of the resulting approach, not a value the plan says has already been reached.
What exactly would the unseen-composition F1 tell us?

It would measure ambiguity detection on unseen compositions, balancing incorrect ambiguity flags against missed ambiguous utterances. The broader target is F1 ≥0.85, judged using independently annotated sets of valid interpretations. A score would tell us how the evaluated decisions performed; the plan supplies no score yet.
Could the head look good on development compositions and still confuse unfamiliarity with ambiguity on unseen ones?

Yes. Calibration on development compositions does not guarantee the same distinction will hold for unseen compositions. That is why the plan explicitly includes unseen-composition F1 evaluation: the head must recognize genuinely multiple interpretations without flagging an utterance merely because its structure is unfamiliar.
If several candidate parses appear on an unseen composition, what should that evaluation be checking?

Whether the ambiguity judgment tracks the annotated valid interpretations, not merely the number of candidates that appeared. If only one interpretation is valid, additional candidates should not be treated as proof of ambiguity. If multiple interpretations are valid, a single preferred execution output should not hide that ambiguity.
Does evaluating F1 also establish execution parity?

No. Ambiguity-detection F1 and execution parity are separate checks. Execution parity concerns unambiguous-input execution accuracy relative to a single-output parser trained on identical data. Strong ambiguity detection alone would not establish that comparison.
Even with a frozen execution parser, should parity still be evaluated?

Yes. Freezing the execution parser is part of the proposed setup, but the plan still calls for evaluating execution parity. The fact that a component is frozen is not a reported measurement of the full system’s unambiguous-input execution accuracy.
Does this plan require a particular architecture for the validity head?
No architecture is specified. The plan says what to train it on, where to calibrate it, and what to evaluate. It leaves the head’s implementation and the precise way it expresses validity open.
Does it settle how to generate the interpretations that the head considers?

No. Annotated interpretation sets and counterfactual negatives are specified as training inputs, but this plan does not prescribe a candidate-generation method for evaluation or deployment. That detail should not be assumed from the plan.
I want to avoid implying that counterfactual negatives are the independent annotations themselves. Are those different roles?

They are different roles in the plan. Annotated interpretation sets identify valid interpretations; counterfactual negatives provide alternatives the head should learn not to accept as valid. The plan does not say that generating a negative changes the independently annotated set of valid interpretations.
What result would speak most directly to the concern that the head mistakes low-confidence alternatives for genuine ambiguity?

The unseen-composition ambiguity evaluation speaks to that concern: it checks whether ambiguity flags align with the annotated valid-interpretation sets despite unfamiliar compositions. In particular, an alternative’s low confidence or an ensemble’s disagreement should not substitute for evidence that it is licensed. The plan calls for evaluating that distinction, without claiming a result in advance.
Should I describe development calibration as a way to guarantee F1 ≥0.85?
No. Calibration is a planned step, not a guarantee. The F1 ≥0.85 target remains something to assess on unseen compositions after calibration; execution parity must also be assessed separately.
Then the sequence is training the head, calibrating its judgments, and testing both ambiguity detection and execution. Is anything in that wording too strong?

That wording fits if ‘testing’ means evaluating rather than presuming success. More precisely: train the validity head on annotated interpretation sets and counterfactual negatives; calibrate on development compositions; then evaluate unseen-composition ambiguity F1 and execution parity. The plan leaves the methods and results of those steps open.

For the evaluation, I want to compare validity heads trained with and without counterfactual negatives on independently annotated CompSplit-1, measuring ambiguity F1 and unambiguous execution parity. What does that comparison test?

It tests whether including counterfactual negatives is associated with better ambiguity detection, while also checking whether unambiguous-input execution remains on par with the relevant single-output parser. The independent annotations on CompSplit-1 provide the reference for judging valid interpretations. This describes the evaluation to perform, not its results.
Why include a validity head without counterfactual negatives?

It gives you a comparison for the contribution of those negatives. Both heads have the same intended task of assessing which interpretations are valid; the contrast asks whether training with counterfactual negatives helps the head reject unsupported alternatives rather than treating them as genuine ambiguity. The comparison does not presuppose that it will help.
Would it be fair to say this isolates the effect of counterfactual negatives?

That is the intended comparison, but attributing a difference specifically to the negatives depends on the heads being comparable in the other respects relevant to evaluation. The activity specifies the with-and-without contrast; it does not give all the controls or implementation details needed to make a stronger causal claim in advance.
What does ‘independently annotated CompSplit-1’ establish for the evaluation?

It identifies CompSplit-1 as the independently annotated evaluation set. Its annotations provide a reference separate from the validity heads’ own predictions, so ambiguity can be judged by valid interpretations rather than by a head’s uncertainty or the mere presence of alternative parses. No annotation procedure or dataset size is specified here.
Should I infer anything else about CompSplit-1 from its name?

No. Its name should be preserved as CompSplit-1, but the name alone does not establish its size, contents, or how its compositions were selected. The stated activity is to evaluate the two validity-head conditions on it.
How should ambiguity F1 be interpreted in this comparison?

It measures how well each head’s ambiguity decisions align with the independently annotated reference, balancing missed ambiguous cases against incorrect ambiguity flags. Comparing F1 for the heads with and without counterfactual negatives addresses whether that training ingredient helps ambiguity detection. The activity reports no F1 values.
Does a head get credit for flagging ambiguity whenever it finds a second candidate?

Not merely for finding one. The relevant distinction is whether multiple interpretations are valid according to the independent annotations. A second candidate that a model proposes but the utterance does not license should not count as genuine ambiguity.
And if it treats a difficult but unambiguous input as ambiguous?

That would be an incorrect ambiguity flag relative to an annotated set with only one valid interpretation. It is precisely the sort of confusion between model uncertainty and utterance ambiguity that the evaluation is meant to detect.
Would rejecting every second interpretation be enough to score well?

Not if the annotations include utterances with multiple valid interpretations. A head that rejects valid additional interpretations would miss genuine ambiguity. F1 matters because the evaluation must account for both incorrect ambiguity flags and missed ambiguous cases.
What is the separate purpose of measuring unambiguous execution parity?

It checks whether unambiguous-input execution accuracy matches the single-output parser comparison, rather than looking only at ambiguity detection. The broader requirement specifies a single-output parser trained on identical data as that baseline. An ambiguity F1 result would not, by itself, answer the execution-parity question.
If the execution parser is frozen, can we simply assume parity?

No. Freezing is part of the proposed approach, but this activity explicitly measures unambiguous execution parity. The measurement is what addresses the requirement; the description does not state that parity has been achieved.
Would execution parity tell me which validity head is better at recognizing ambiguity?

No. Parity concerns execution accuracy on unambiguous inputs. Ambiguity F1 concerns the validity heads’ ambiguity judgments. Both are measured because a system could differ on one dimension without that alone settling the other.
Can I describe the comparison as a test of the hypothesis about ensemble-only alternatives?

Yes, as an evaluation of that hypothesis, not confirmation of it. Counterfactual negatives are hypothesized to help the head reject alternatives that arise from ensemble disagreement without being valid interpretations.
